records.content: Targeting MPXV I7L Protease: Promising New Antiviral Strategy for, Suggests Review A recent clinical review published in the Indian Journal of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology in July 2026 reveals that targeting the monkeypox virus (MPXV) I7L core protease with inhibitors like A68, shikonin, and myricetin could revolutionize how clinicians combat this global health threat. Although targeting the monkeypox virus (MPXV) I7L core protease is a promising antiviral strategy, its clinical translation is hindered by poorly understood safety and selectivity profiles. To bridge this gap, Hinpetch Daungsupawong of Laos and Viroj Wiwanitkit of Saveetha University in India reviewed these key challenges to outline a clear path toward effective treatments. Therefore, the clinical review was designed as a scientific perspective and qualitative literature analysis, rather than an empirical trial, meaning it utilized no clinical population, sample size, trial duration, or clinical exclusion criteria. Instead, the authors evaluated published molecular data on I7L core protease inhibitors, focusing on translating in vitro potency to in vivo efficacy as the primary analytical endpoint. Key Clinical Findings of the Study Includes: • Inhibitor Profiles Compared: Investigators reviewed how the synthetic covalent inhibitor A68 demonstrates high in vitro potency, whereas natural compounds like shikonin and myricetin show only moderate enzymatic inhibition. • Structural Binding Gaps: Researchers highlighted that shikonin suffers from unconfirmed structural binding and poor bioavailability, while myricetin lacks specificity data against the viral protease. • Repurposing Toxicity Risks: Reviewers cautioned that repurposed compounds originally designed for coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) require extensive off-target toxicity screening to prevent unintended interactions with human proteins. • In Vivo Pharmacokinetic Obstacles: Analysts emphasized that preclinical animal testing is critical to evaluate whether these promising molecules can reach therapeutic concentrations in serum and target tissues. • Synergistic Combination Therapies: Authors proposed that combining protease inhibitors with immunomodulators or vaccines can optimize treatment outcomes by simultaneously boosting immune responses and blocking replication. The results suggest that targeting the I7L core protease represents a highly viable antiviral strategy, but translating this to a clinical reality requires addressing key research gaps in structure-function relationships, in vivo pharmacokinetics, and off-target safety profiles. Expanding compound databases and implementing synergistic combination regimens will be essential steps to accelerate the delivery of safe, optimized therapies for future outbreak control. Thus, the review concludes clinicians should consider that managing monkeypox infections effectively may ultimately depend on a multi-pronged therapeutic approach that combines protease inhibitors with other antiviral strategies, such as vaccines and immunomodulatory agents, rather than relying on monotherapy. Although the review is currently limited by the lack of living-organism data for these protease inhibitors, it highlights an urgent clinical opportunity to transition these compounds into animal model testing to resolve their precise in vivo safety, bioavailability, and therapeutic dosing schedules. Reference Daungsupawong H, Wiwanitkit V. Targeting the monkeypox virus: Protease inhibitors, selectivity, and in vivo efficacy. Indian J Allergy Asthma Immunol 2026;40:9-11

Home Pakistan International Business Sports Lifestyle Sci & Tech Blogs Health Off Beat Health Karachi reports new monkeypox case By Anwar Khan - Sep 04, 2026 Add ARY News on Google Image Credit: Health News Hub AA Resize KARACHI: Another case of monkeypox has been diagnosed in Karachi, bringing the city’s total number of confirmed cases to 41, ARY News reported. A 19-year-old youth from interior Sindh was diagnosed with the disease and admitted to NIPA Hospital yesterday. A PCR test subsequently confirmed the presence of monkeypox in the young patient. The patient is currently receiving treatment in the isolation ward at NIPA Hospital. Earlier, a case of Monkeypox (mpox) had been reported in Gulistan-e-Johar, Karachi, Pakistan, according to hospital authorities. A 40-year-old man, a resident of Gulistan-e-Johar, has tested positive for the mpox virus and is currently undergoing treatment in the isolation ward (ICU) of NIPA Hospital. Hospital officials said the patient had no recent travel history. The infection was confirmed through a PCR test. With the latest case, the number of mpox patients treated at NIPA Hospital has risen to seven, while the total number of reported cases of mpox in Karachi has reached 10. Monkeypox is an illness caused by the monkeypox virus. It is a viral zoonotic infection, meaning that it can spread from animals to humans. It can also spread from humans to other humans and from the environment to humans. The monkeypox virus was discovered in Denmark (1958) in monkeys kept for research and the first reported human case of mpox was a nine-month-old boy in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC, 1970). Mpox can spread from person to person or occasionally from animals to people. Following eradication of smallpox in 1980 and the end of smallpox vaccination worldwide, mpox steadily emerged in central, east and west Africa. A global outbreak occurred in 2022–2023. The natural reservoir of the virus is unknown – various small mammals such as squirrels and monkeys are susceptible. records.content: Sunday, September 6, 2026 Menu #EndSARS Politics Anti-Corruption Rights Economy Education Health Sport Nationwide Opinion Search #EndSARS Politics Anti-Corruption Rights Economy Education Health Sport Nationwide Opinion Menu Global mpox vaccine stockpile begins operations in September According to the statement, two-thirds of reported cases occurred in Africa. Olumayowa Samuel • September 2, 2026 Monkeypox used to illustrate the story [Credit: The Health Site] A global mpox vaccine stockpile will begin operations in September in a bid to ensure that all countries have access to vaccines when responding to mpox outbreaks. In a statement on Wednesday, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi), said the commencement of operations follows the launch of a global initiative to establish the stockpile on August 27, 2026. The statement read, “Set to begin operations later this month, this new global mpox vaccine stockpile that all countries can access is a resource that was approved by the Board of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi) in 2025, and is funded by Gavi and coordinated by the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision. The ICG partners are the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the World Health Organization (WHO). “The initiative builds on the Access and Allocation Mechanism established in 2024 during the last mpox Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC), and will ensure that countries have timely and equitable access to vaccines for outbreak response.” According to the statement, two-thirds of reported cases occurred in Africa, while from January 1, 2022, to July 31, 2026, 145 countries and territories reported 190,683 confirmed cases and 529 deaths. Speaking on the development, the CEO of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, Sania Nishtar, stated that the 2022 mpox outbreak witnessed low-income countries being left behind in terms of access to vaccines, prompting the need for a mechanism to ensure they can be accessed by those who need them most. Mr Nishtar further stated that, “Core to the Gavi Leap approach is increasing our responsiveness to country needs, and the bottom line is that any country in the world – not just those with the ability to pay the most – should be able to use this tool to save lives. “That is why Gavi supported the international response to the 2024 global mpox emergency by securing rapid access to doses through our First Response Fund, and why our Board agreed to establish and finance a global stockpile managed by our ICG partners. Our hope is that this stockpile will keep the world safer from the threat of this deadly disease.” Secretary-General and CEO of the IFRC, Jagan Chapagain, stated that, “Mpox is a horrible illness so I’m pleased that we’ve got to this important step in the battle to control it. Access to vaccines – for all who need them – is absolutely vital. That’s why this global coordination mechanism and vaccine stockpile matters. Both will help ensure vaccines reach the people and communities at greatest risk – when and where they are needed most. This is rare good news.” On her part, the International Medical Coordinator at MSF, Daniela Garone, welcomed the establishment of the vaccine stockpile under the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision, which allows for the equitable allocation of vaccines based on demand and impact in controlling disease outbreaks. Mrs Garone added, “The distinctive nature of mpox, with the coexistence of different variants that affect different populations, now demands a close collaboration between country, regional and global mechanisms as well as between disease programmes, health managers, communities and public health partners to reach more people with mpox vaccines.” UNICEF executive director Catherine Russell noted that, “Mpox can be devastating for children – not just its physical effects, but also the stigma, interrupted learning, and fear that can come with being isolated from family and friends. This vital initiative will help us quickly get vaccines to the children, families, and communities most at risk of the disease.” WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus described the launch as “an important step towards a more sustainable and equitable approach to mpox outbreak response,” adding that, “by establishing a dedicated global stockpile, using an approach that has proven successful for managing other emergency vaccines, we are ensuring that countries can access them more quickly when they need them, saving lives and containing outbreaks before they spread further.” The statement said mpox is a viral disease that spreads primarily through close physical contact between people, while animal-to-human transmission continues to occur in parts of Africa, contributing to the ongoing risk of new outbreaks. The statement explained that mpox can cause severe disease, especially in children and people with suppressed immune systems, adding that by protecting people at risk of infection and severe disease, vaccines help contain mpox outbreaks more quickly, prevent severe illness, and save lives. (File photo: Department of Disease Control New cases of monkey pox (Mpox) and coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) continue to rise since June with the presence of a severer mpox strain and a low fatality rate for Covid-19, according to the Department of Disease Control. Dr Montien Kanasawat, director-general of the department, said on Wednesday that from Jan 1 to Aug 23, Thailand recorded 254 Mpox cases, including 193 cases of the Clade Ib strain and 58 cases of the Clade II strain. Patients were in Greater Bangkok, big cities and tourist provinces. Transmission resulted from sexual intercourses, which were related to visits to closed and crowded places. Dr Montien said the Mpox situation in Thailand remained controllable and the number of cases was rising for the Clade Ib strain, which caused more severe symptoms than the Clade II strain especially in patients with low immunity. Symptoms include fever, headache, swollen lymph nodes and rashes. Regarding Covid-19 infection, Dr Jurai Wongsawat, spokeswoman of the Department of Disease Control, said from Jan 1 to Aug 31 there were about 99,000 cases. Records showed that there were more cases since June due to the conditions of the wet season but total cases were lower than figures in the past three years. She said that the current fatality rate among Covid-19 patients was at 0.02% and most deaths were patients above the age of 60. There had not been a child fatality this year as there were enough medicine and efficient treatment systems, which limited symptoms, Dr Jurai added. Vaccination, good personal hygiene and avoiding close contact with infected people or contaminated surfaces are key to preventing both coronavirus and mpox. Covid-19 mainly spreads through respiratory droplets, whereas mpox spreads primarily through close, skin-to-skin contact. A 19-year-old youth from interior Sindh was diagnosed with the disease and admitted to NIPA Hospital yesterday. A PCR test subsequently confirmed the presence of monkeypox in the young patient. The patient is currently receiving treatment in the isolation ward at NIPA Hospital. Earlier, a case of Monkeypox (mpox) had been reported in Gulistan-e-Johar, Karachi, Pakistan, according to hospital authorities. A 40-year-old man, a resident of Gulistan-e-Johar, has tested positive for the mpox virus and is currently undergoing treatment in the isolation ward (ICU) of NIPA Hospital. Hospital officials said the patient had no recent travel history. The infection was confirmed through a PCR test. With the latest case, the number of mpox patients treated at NIPA Hospital has risen to seven, while the total number of reported cases of mpox in Karachi has reached 10. Monkeypox is an illness caused by the monkeypox virus. It is a viral zoonotic infection, meaning that it can spread from animals to humans. It can also spread from humans to other humans and from the environment to humans. The monkeypox virus was discovered in Denmark (1958) in monkeys kept for research and the first reported human case of mpox was a nine-month-old boy in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC, 1970). Mpox can spread from person to person or occasionally from animals to people. Following eradication of smallpox in 1980 and the end of smallpox vaccination worldwide, mpox steadily emerged in central, east and west Africa. A global outbreak occurred in 2022–2023. The natural reservoir of the virus is unknown – various small mammals such as squirrels and monkeys are susceptible. records.content: A person suffering from Mpox/FILE Kenya will benefit from a new global stockpile of Mpox vaccines that will help countries get the jabs faster when outbreaks occur. The stockpile was launched on August 27 and is expected to begin operations later this month. It has been created to make sure that countries can get Mpox vaccines quickly and fairly, especially when infections start rising. The initiative is funded by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, and will be coordinated by the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision. The ICG brings together the World Health Organisation, Unicef, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies and Médecins Sans Frontières. “During the 2022 Mpox outbreak, lower-income countries were left behind when it came to access to vaccines," Gavi CEO Dr Sania Nishtar said. "It was clear that a mechanism was needed to ensure this global public good could be accessed by those who need it most.” WHO director general Dr Tedros Ghebreyesus called the launch an important step towards a more sustainable and equitable approach to fighting Mpox outbreaks. “By establishing a dedicated global stockpile, using an approach that has proven successful for managing other emergency vaccines, we are ensuring that countries can access them more quickly when they need them, saving lives and containing outbreaks before they spread further,” he said. Kenya's own experience with Mpox shows why this matters. Earlier this year, WHO data showed Kenya recording the highest number of Mpox deaths in Africa over a six-week stretch between February and March 2026, even though the country did not have the most cases. Four people died out of 78 confirmed cases in that period alone. However, the most recent WHO report, published on July 31, paints a somewhat different picture. Over the six weeks leading up to July 19, Kenya recorded 48 confirmed Mpox cases and no deaths, placing it third among African countries after Madagascar and Angola. This suggests Kenya's outbreak has eased compared to earlier in the year, even though it remains among the countries WHO is watching closely. Madagascar remains by far the worst-hit country on the continent. It has reported nearly 3,000 confirmed cases and 18 deaths since December 2025, the largest Mpox outbreak anywhere in Africa or the world right now. The island nation has vaccinated close to 90,000 people, including health workers, sex workers and people living with HIV, though the outbreak is not yet under control. Across Africa as a whole, 32 countries reported more than 51,000 confirmed Mpox cases and 235 deaths between January 2025 and mid-July 2026. Globally, Mpox has affected 105 countries, with more than 63,000 confirmed cases and 256 deaths recorded since the start of 2025. Mpox spreads mainly through close physical contact with an infected person, including through sex, and sometimes through contact with infected animals. It can cause fever, painful skin rashes and swollen lymph nodes. The illness can be especially dangerous for young children and people with weak immune systems, such as those living with untreated HIV. Health officials say vaccination remains one of the most effective ways to protect people at high risk and stop outbreaks from spreading further. With the new global stockpile now in place, Kenya and other African countries facing Mpox outbreaks should find it easier and faster to get vaccine doses when they are needed, rather than competing with wealthier nations for limited supplies. WHO urged countries, including Kenya, to strengthen surveillance, expand testing and keep the public informed, as the disease continues to circulate in communities across the continent. Health experts note that Mpox spreads more easily where surveillance is weak and testing is limited, meaning true case numbers in some counties could be higher than what is officially reported. “Mpox can be devastating for children, not just its physical effects, but also the stigma, interrupted learning and fear that can come with being isolated from family and friends," Unicef executive director Catherine Russell said. "This vital initiative will help us quickly get vaccines to the children, families and communities most at risk of the disease."

records.content: Three new monkeypox cases reported from Karachi Monkeypox has resurfaced in Sindh province with three new confirmed cases, including a man and his daughter, pushing the provincial tally to 40, according to 24NewsHD TV channel on Friday. According to hospital sources at Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital in NIPA, PCR tests confirmed Mpox in three patients currently under treatment. One additional suspected case has been reported and test results are awaited. Of the three newly confirmed cases, two patients belong to interior Sindh and are a father and daughter. The third confirmed patient is a 46-year-old man from Karachi's Federal B Area. Officials said the final situation will be clear once the report of the suspected patient is received. With the latest cases, the total number of confirmed Mpox cases in the province has reached 40, including 13 from Karachi. Health experts said Mpox is a viral disease caused by a virus from the same family as the smallpox virus. The prominent symptoms include rash, painful or itchy lesions, fever, headache, body aches and fatigue. In some patients, lymph nodes in the neck, armpits or groin may also swell. The Mpox rash can appear on different parts of the body, including the face, hands, feet, mouth and throat. Some patients may not show any clear symptoms before the lesions appear. It can take up to 21 days for symptoms to appear after exposure to the virus. Reporter: Ibrahim Rind

records.content: TODAY’S PAPER | September 07, 2026 | EPAPER ☰ Home Latest Pakistan Business World Sports Opinion Life & Style T-Magazine Blogs Tech Cartoon Home Sindh Mpox resurfaces as man, daughter among 3 new cases Some patients may not show any clear symptoms before the lesions appear Faran Khan September 04, 2026 1 min read facebook twitter whatsup linkded email K-P reported first locally transmitted MPOX case. PHOTO: FILE KARACHI: Mpox has resurfaced in Sindh with three new confirmed cases, including a man and his daughter, pushing the provincial tally to 40. According to hospital sources at Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital in NIPA, PCR tests confirmed Mpox in three patients currently under treatment. One additional suspected case has been reported and test results are awaited. Of the three newly confirmed cases, two patients belong to interior Sindh and are a father and daughter. The third confirmed patient is a 46-year-old man from Karachi's Federal B Area. Officials said the final situation will be clear once the report of the suspected patient is received. With the latest cases, the total number of confirmed Mpox cases in the province has reached 40, including 13 from Karachi. Health experts said Mpox is a viral disease caused by a virus from the same family as the smallpox virus. The prominent symptoms include rash, painful or itchy lesions, fever, headache, body aches and fatigue. In some patients, lymph nodes in the neck, armpits or groin may also swell. The Mpox rash can appear on different parts of the body, including the face, hands, feet, mouth and throat. Some patients may not show any clear symptoms before the lesions appear. Targeting MPXV I7L Protease: Promising New Antiviral Strategy for, Suggests Review Written By : Aashi verma Published On 2026-09-02T21:00:02+05:30 | Updated On 3 Sept 2026 2:59 PM IST A recent clinical review published in the Indian Journal of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology in July 2026 reveals that targeting the monkeypox virus (MPXV) I7L core protease with inhibitors like A68, shikonin, and myricetin could revolutionize how clinicians combat this global health threat. Although targeting the monkeypox virus (MPXV) I7L core protease is a promising antiviral strategy, its clinical translation is hindered by poorly understood safety and selectivity profiles. To bridge this gap, Hinpetch Daungsupawong of Laos and Viroj Wiwanitkit of Saveetha University in India reviewed these key challenges to outline a clear path toward effective treatments. Therefore, the clinical review was designed as a scientific perspective and qualitative literature analysis, rather than an empirical trial, meaning it utilized no clinical population, sample size, trial duration, or clinical exclusion criteria. Instead, the authors evaluated published molecular data on I7L core protease inhibitors, focusing on translating in vitro potency to in vivo efficacy as the primary analytical endpoint. Key Clinical Findings of the Study Includes: • Inhibitor Profiles Compared: Investigators reviewed how the synthetic covalent inhibitor A68 demonstrates high in vitro potency, whereas natural compounds like shikonin and myricetin show only moderate enzymatic inhibition. • Structural Binding Gaps: Researchers highlighted that shikonin suffers from unconfirmed structural binding and poor bioavailability, while myricetin lacks specificity data against the viral protease. • Repurposing Toxicity Risks: Reviewers cautioned that repurposed compounds originally designed for coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) require extensive off-target toxicity screening to prevent unintended interactions with human proteins. • In Vivo Pharmacokinetic Obstacles: Analysts emphasized that preclinical animal testing is critical to evaluate whether these promising molecules can reach therapeutic concentrations in serum and target tissues. • Synergistic Combination Therapies: Authors proposed that combining protease inhibitors with immunomodulators or vaccines can optimize treatment outcomes by simultaneously boosting immune responses and blocking replication. The results suggest that targeting the I7L core protease represents a highly viable antiviral strategy, but translating this to a clinical reality requires addressing key research gaps in structure-function relationships, in vivo pharmacokinetics, and off-target safety profiles. Expanding compound databases and implementing synergistic combination regimens will be essential steps to accelerate the delivery of safe, optimized therapies for future outbreak control. Thus, the review concludes clinicians should consider that managing monkeypox infections effectively may ultimately depend on a multi-pronged therapeutic approach that combines protease inhibitors with other antiviral strategies, such as vaccines and immunomodulatory agents, rather than relying on monotherapy. Although the review is currently limited by the lack of living-organism data for these protease inhibitors, it highlights an urgent clinical opportunity to transition these compounds into animal model testing to resolve their precise in vivo safety, bioavailability, and therapeutic dosing schedules. Reference Daungsupawong H, Wiwanitkit V. Targeting the monkeypox virus: Protease inhibitors, selectivity, and in vivo efficacy. Indian J Allergy Asthma Immunol 2026;40:9-11.
